summary.text: A flower is the reproductive structure of a flowering plant, typically built in four circular levels around the end of a stalk.
Sepals support the flower, petals often attract pollinators, stamens present pollen, and the female gynoecia receive it.
After pollination and fertilisation, the resulting cell grows into a seed while the female part of the flower forms a fruit and the other floral structures die.

facts.label: Cone equivalent
facts.value: Cones are the gymnosperm counterpart of flowers

items.prompt: A bee lands on a flower and gets dusted with pollen from the tip of a slender organ. Which part presented that pollen?

options.label: The female gynoecia
The male stamens
The supporting sepals
The showy petals

items.explain: Stamens are the male parts where pollen is presented; gynoecia are the female parts that receive it.

items.prompt: A plant relies on insects to carry its pollen. Why would it have brightly coloured petals?

options.label: Their colour and form help draw pollinators in
They hold the egg cell safe inside the flower
They support the whole flower on its stalk
They grow into the fruit after pollination

items.explain: Petals are often designed to attract pollinators, and the colour and structure of flowers assist pollination.

items.prompt: Why do plants tend to favour cross-pollination over self-pollination?

options.label: It lets the flower skip fertilisation altogether
It keeps every offspring identical to its parent
It makes the fruit ripen much more quickly
It joins sex cells from different plants, adding diversity

items.explain: Cross-pollination brings together sex cells from genetically distinct plants of the same species, which increases genetic diversity.

items.prompt: A flower has just been pollinated and fertilised. What soon happens to its female part?

options.label: It grows into a fresh bud on the same stalk
It dies back along with the other floral structures
It forms a fruit while the other floral structures die
It turns into a sepal that wraps the seed

items.explain: After fertilisation the female part of the flower forms a fruit, and the other floral structures die.

items.prompt: A bird eats a fruit and drops the seeds later in a faraway spot. What job of the fruit does this show?

options.label: Carrying pollen between separate flowers
Guarding the seed and spreading it away from the parent
Turning pollen into a seed
Feeding the embryo before it is fertilised

items.explain: The function of fruit is to protect the seed and aid in its dispersal, and living things such as birds can spread the seeds.

items.prompt: Flowering plants replaced non-flowering plants in many ecosystems. What explains this?

options.label: They evolved before any other kind of plant
They grew far larger than non-flowering plants
They no longer needed pollination to make seeds
Flowers made them more effective at reproducing

items.explain: Plants with flowers replaced non-flowering plants in many ecosystems as a result of flowers' superior reproductive effectiveness.
